The word median always points to the same underlying idea: the middle — specifically, the point or value that sits exactly at the halfway mark, dividing something into two equal halves. It appears in three important contexts.

This is the most widely used sense of the word.

When you have a list of numbers, the median is the middle value after you've sorted the list from smallest to largest.

Take these five numbers: 3, 8, 12, 20, 45. The middle one is 12. Two numbers sit below it (3 and 8), and two sit above it (20 and 45). So the median is 12.

What if the list has an even number of values? Then there's no single middle value. You take the two values closest to the center and find their average. For example: 4, 10, 16, 22. The two middle values are 10 and 16. Their average is (10 + 16) ÷ 2 = 13. So the median is 13 — even though 13 doesn't actually appear in the list.
How the Median Differs From the Mean

Most people learn the word "average" in school — add all numbers up and divide by how many there are. In mathematics, this is called the mean. The median and the mean are both ways of describing the "center" of a group of numbers, but they behave very differently, and understanding this difference is one of the most important things about the word median.

The mean is easily pulled off course by extreme values. The median is not.

Imagine six people work at a small company with these annual salaries:

$28,000 · $31,000 · $35,000 · $38,000 · $40,000 · $600,000

The mean salary is roughly $128,667. But look — five of the six employees earn far below that figure. The one enormous salary has dragged the mean far away from where most people actually sit.

The median tells a different story. The two middle values are $35,000 and $38,000. The median is ($35,000 + $38,000) ÷ 2 = $36,500. That is a far more honest picture of what a typical employee earns.

This is precisely why economists and journalists prefer to report median household income rather than mean household income. The median isn't distorted by the ultra-wealthy at one extreme. It tells you what someone in the actual middle of the pack is experiencing.

As a general rule: when a dataset has outliers (unusually high or low values that are far from the rest), the median is a better and fairer measure of the "typical" value than the mean.

One more layer worth knowing: the median is also the 50th percentile. This just means that exactly 50% of values in a dataset fall below it, and 50% fall above it. It is the dead center of any dataset.
In Geometry — The Median of a Triangle

In geometry, a median has a specific meaning. When you draw a straight line from one corner (called a vertex) of a triangle to the exact midpoint of the opposite side, that line is called a median of the triangle.

Every triangle has three vertices, so every triangle has exactly three medians — one from each corner.

Here is something elegant: no matter the shape of the triangle — whether it's long and thin, perfectly equilateral, or wildly irregular — all three medians always meet at exactly one point inside the triangle. This point is called the centroid. The centroid is also the triangle's center of gravity: if you cut the triangle out of a piece of uniform cardboard, the centroid is the exact point where you could balance it perfectly on the tip of a pencil.

In everyday American English, a median (also called a median strip) refers to the dividing section that runs down the center of a road, separating traffic moving in opposite directions. It can be a strip of grass, a concrete barrier, a guardrail, a raised curb, or simply a painted zone. Its purpose is to keep opposing streams of traffic safely apart. British English often calls this a central reservation instead.
The One Thread That Ties Everything Together

All three uses come back to the same core idea: the middle — the point that lies exactly between two halves. In statistics, the median divides the lower half of a dataset from the upper half. In geometry, the median connects a corner of a triangle to the midpoint of the opposite side. On a road, the median physically divides two opposing directions of travel. Whatever the context, the median is always about the middle.
